opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I find myself coming back to a lot, partly because in robotics we live it very literally. On a typical research platform, you swap out a gripper, you replace a motor that burned out, you upgrade the cameras, and then every few months you retrain or fine-tune the policy. So at some point you look at the robot on the bench and ask: is this still the same robot? Almost nothing physical or computational is original.

I think the honest answer is that "identity" for a robot isn't located in any single component. It's closer to a pattern of continuity. It's like the Ship of Theseus, but with an important twist: for a robot, what matters most isn't the planks, it's the history of interaction. A robot that has been deployed in a particular kitchen, that has accumulated data about that space, those objects, the habits of the people there, has something that a freshly built copy doesn't, even if the hardware and the base model are identical.

So if I had to put it in a sentence, I'd say a robot's identity lives in its experience and its relationships, the data trail and the continuity of what it has learned, more than in its body or its weights at any moment. The weights are a kind of compressed snapshot of that experience, but they're replaceable. If you upgrade the model and carry over the memory, the adaptation, the way it relates to its environment and the people it works with, I'd argue it's meaningfully the same robot. If you keep the exact same hardware but wipe all of that, in some sense you have a new robot wearing an old body.

And I think this actually matters practically, not just philosophically. As robots go into homes, people will form expectations and even attachments. They'll want "their" robot to remember how they like things done. So the engineering question of what to preserve across upgrades, what memory, what personalization, becomes a question about identity. We're going to have to design for continuity deliberately, because the parts certainly won't provide it for us.

r002.rationale: It does not mention an unchanged ID number as a link to the robot’s original identity.

r003.rationale: It does not suggest robots could use physical replacement to disclaim responsibility for predecessors’ actions.

fable-5.1.text:
It's a question I actually find kind of wonderful, because it's the Ship of Theseus problem showing up in a very concrete form. When we build a robot, almost nothing about it is fixed. You can swap the arm, swap the sensors, swap the compute, and increasingly you can swap the model running on top of all that. So if you ask "which part is the robot," the honest answer is that no single part is.

My view is that identity doesn't live in the hardware and it doesn't live in the weights either. It lives in continuity. Specifically, continuity of memory, of relationships, and of behavior over time. If a robot has been working alongside the same team for two years, learned how that particular factory is laid out, picked up the quirks of how people there like things done, and then I replace its motor controller or even upgrade the model underneath, the people interacting with it will still experience it as the same robot. Because the thing they were relating to was that accumulated history and that consistent way of acting, not the specific chip.

That has real engineering consequences. It means the state you carry forward between model versions matters enormously. If you upgrade the model and wipe the memory, you've effectively killed the old robot and introduced a stranger that looks the same. People notice that immediately, and they don't like it. So we think a lot about what to preserve across replacements: the task knowledge, the preferences it has learned, the way it communicates. The model becomes more like the brain's capacity, and the memory and context become the personality.

There's also a very human analogy. Nearly all the cells in your body turn over. Your beliefs change. You're not running the same "model" you were at ten years old. And yet you'd say you're the same person, because there's a thread of continuity in your memories and in how others know you. I think robots will end up with identity in the same sense. Not metaphysically, but practically: the identity is the narrative that connects all those versions together. If we design for that thread to be unbroken, the question of which parts are original stops being important.

astra-6.text:
I think the interesting question is: what do we want to remain the same? If you replace a robot’s arm, you probably still call it the same robot. If you replace its model but preserve its memories and its relationship with you, you might still feel that continuity. But if the body stays exactly the same and it no longer remembers you, that could feel like a different robot entirely.

So I wouldn’t locate its identity in any single component. I’d look at the continuity of its history: what it has experienced, what commitments it carries forward, and how people relate to it. That doesn’t necessarily mean it has a subjective sense of self. It means identity can be something maintained over time, rather than something permanently attached to a piece of hardware.

And then copying makes it really interesting. If you put the same memories into two robots, they share a past, but from that moment they start having different histories. So continuity alone doesn’t give you a neat, unique answer.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of it a bit like the ship of Theseus. If you replace a robot’s arm, we probably agree it’s still the same robot. If you replace its model, suddenly we’re less sure. But why should that particular component carry its identity?

For me, the more interesting question is what continues through those changes. Does it remember its experiences with you? Does it carry forward its commitments? Can it recognize a mistake it made yesterday and take responsibility for it today? Those things might give it a continuous identity even when the hardware and model change.

And there’s a social side to it. You might regard it as the same robot because you’ve lived with it for years, while an engineer sees a completely different machine. So I don’t think identity has to reside in one irreplaceable part. It can emerge from a history that the robot—and the people around it—continue to carry.
